titre: The Clause Written Not to Settle a Disagreement
accroche: In 1899 at The Hague, delegations clash over the fate of irregular combatants. A Russian jurist breaks the deadlock with a sentence that settles nothing.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1899, the delegations gathered at The Hague for the first Peace Conference run into a question that blocks the whole negotiation: what to do with the inhabitants of an occupied territory who take up arms without wearing a uniform? The great military powers, including Russia and Germany, want to be able to treat them as francs-tireurs (irregular fighters) and execute them summarily. The small states, led by Belgium and more vulnerable to occupation, want instead to recognize them as regular combatants. No compromise text satisfies both camps.

## A sentence that refers the question rather than answering it

It is the Russian jurist and diplomat Fyodor Martens who unblocks the negotiation, proposing not a rule on the substance but a clause of method, inserted in the preamble of the convention. It says that in the absence of a precise written rule, populations and belligerents remain under the protection of the principles of the law of nations as they result from the usages established between civilized nations, from the laws of humanity, and from the requirements of the public conscience.

The clause does not say what to do with irregular combatants. It says that where there is no agreement on that precise point, the treaty's silence is not the law's silence: general principles keep applying, even when no article states them. This is what allows the delegates to sign the convention without having settled their disagreement, each one remaining free to defend his own reading of customary law on the ground they failed to cover with a common text.

## A clause designed against the legal vacuum

What the episode shifts is the idea that an incomplete treaty would leave a void in which everything becomes permitted. The Martens clause asserts the opposite: the absence of a specific rule does not open a lawless space; it refers back to more general principles that continue to apply. This function, filling by principle what a text does not cover in writing, explains its survival well beyond the 1899 disagreement over francs-tireurs. The 1907 convention on the laws of war on land takes up the clause in an almost identical preamble, and a reworded version still appears in the first Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions of 1977, more than a century after the conference that produced it so as not to have to choose between two camps.

carte.punch: A clause written in 1899 not to settle a disagreement, and which outlived it.
carte.idee: In 1899 at The Hague, delegations clash over the fate of irregular combatants. Russian jurist Fyodor Martens proposes a clause of method: in the absence of a written rule, the general principles of law keep applying. It still appears in humanitarian law today.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Confirms that the clause is attributed by name to Fyodor Martens, who first introduced it in the preamble of the 1899 convention, and its reuse in other instruments of international humanitarian law.

quiz.question: Why does the clause proposed by Fyodor Martens in 1899 allow the delegations to sign the convention despite their disagreement over irregular combatants?
choix: Because it now explicitly prohibits the summary execution of any combatant without a uniform
Because it affirms that the treaty's silence on this point refers back to general principles rather than to a legal vacuum
Because it entrusts the question to a permanent tribunal created for that purpose by the conference
Because it simply postpones the question to the next conference, planned for 1907
quiz.explication: The clause does not settle the substance of the disagreement over irregular combatants: it affirms that, in the absence of a precise written rule, the general principles of the law of nations keep applying. It is this clause of method, not a compromise on the substance or a referral to a tribunal, that makes it possible to sign without having decided.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the disagreement blocking the negotiation at the 1899 Hague conference?
choix: The status of inhabitants of an occupied territory who take up arms without a uniform
The number of delegates each country could send to the conference
The location of the next peace conference
The official language in which to draft the text of the convention
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry says the negotiation was stuck on the fate of irregular combatants, not on a question of representation, location, or language, which it never mentions.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which countries opposed recognizing regular combatant status for resisters in an occupied territory, in 1899?
choix: The neutral states, which refused to take sides in the debate
The great military powers, including Russia and Germany
The Ottoman Empire alone, absent from the rest of the discussions
The European colonies, not represented at the conference
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the great powers, including Russia and Germany, wanted to treat irregular combatants as francs-tireurs subject to summary execution, against the small states led by Belgium.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which text does the Martens clause reappear, more than a century after the 1899 conference?
choix: The Rome Statute establishing the International Criminal Court in 1998
The 1977 first Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions
The 1929 Geneva Convention on the treatment of prisoners of war
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that a reworded version of the clause still appears in the first Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions of 1977, more than a century after the 1899 conference.
